info.title: Introspection Control Plane API
info.description:
Control Plane for the Introspection agent platform.

The Control Plane owns identity, organizations, projects, recipes, runtimes, experiments, judges, and deployment lifecycle. Task execution and telemetry (tasks, conversations, events, metrics, files) live on the **Data Plane API** of each deployment.

To find a Data Plane: `GET /v1/deployments` returns each deployment's `endpoint`; its API base URL is `https://api.{endpoint}` and each deployment serves its own OpenAPI spec at `https://api.{endpoint}/openapi.json`.

get.description: Get the current user's organization.
List integrations for the authenticated user's organization.

List members for the authenticated user's organization.

The two anchor filters are the two ways a ``customer`` member is minted, and
a member carries at most one of them. ``connector_id`` is how a connector's
channels and DMs are read: a verified chat delivery mints one ``customer``
member per channel, anchored to the connector, so a connector's
conversations are a filter on this list rather than a nested route.
``application_idp_id`` is the federation-side mirror — an application's
customers are read by listing its IdPs and filtering on each, since the
application is the IdP's parent and not a column on this table.

``tag`` spans both: a customer with two Slack workspaces has member keys
sharing no prefix, so neither anchor filter reaches them together and a tag
is the only thing that does. It is also the audit read for tag sharing —
a member tag is access-bearing (docs/design/shared-tags.md), so "who can
reach the rows tagged ``team:acme``" is this filter.

``metadata`` narrows by exact `key:value` containment and grants nothing.

``id`` and ``external_user_id`` are the resolve-a-known-set filters, and
they **union** rather than intersect — see ``MemberRepository.list_paginated``.
They are what lets a telemetry-derived surface (the Users page) turn a page
of opaque owner keys into named subjects in one request instead of one
request per row, which is why they are bounded rather than unbounded: a
resolve is for a page you are already showing, and enumeration is what the
unfiltered list with its cursor is for.

post.description:
Create a new member and invite them via Zitadel.

Creates the user in Zitadel first (validates the email domain is not
reserved by another org), then pre-creates the member record
(no external_user_id yet). When the user logs in, they'll be matched
by email and associated with this org.

A ``customer`` member is instead the org's own end user, keyed by the
``user:``/``anon:`` id a runner identity asserts. It is minted at the same
derived id that assertion would reach, with no invite, so an owner can set
its attributes before its first session; repeating the create returns it.

post.description:
Generate a Data Plane JWT token for a project.

Accepts both DP service tokens and authenticated OIDC user tokens. The issued token embeds
the org_id and project_id, which the Data Plane uses for tenant isolation.
Scope is propagated from the auth context.

When include_refresh_token=true, also creates a refresh token that can be
used with the OAuth /token endpoint (grant_type=refresh_token) to get new
access tokens without re-authenticating.

`environment` names the lane the token belongs to. DP stamps the resulting
browser session cookie after that claim
(`docs/design/environment-scoped-browser-sessions.md`), so it is what lets
one operator hold a `development`, `staging` and `production` DP session
concurrently in a single browser. Only a human OIDC session may name a lane
other than its own credential's — the identical rule
`POST /v1/runtimes/{id}/run` applies to runner mints, and for the same
reason: an operator already reaches every lane of their project through the
UI, while a machine credential's lane is a property of the credential.
Omitting it leaves the claim unset, which DP reads as `production`.

With no ``expires_in`` (or ``0``) the key is soft-deleted and its DP cache

post.description:
Add an identity provider to an existing application.

What may be attached follows the application type: a `jwks` app takes
external `direct_jwks` rows (nothing to provision — `active` immediately),
an `spa` takes brokered rows or the built-in hosted login (provisioned in
Zitadel async; the row starts `pending`), and a `native` app takes
Introspection accounts only. A `service_account` takes none. The brokered
IdP's `client_secret` is encrypted at rest and never returned. Fails with
409 if the application already holds the maximum number of active IdPs.
High-risk (federates an external IdP), so owner-only and gated behind the
`allow_federated_idps` entitlement (Max/Enterprise or developer).

Judges cannot be created here — author a `judges/<name>.yaml` in the

referenced by experiments and emitted by runtime judgements. The lineage
fields describe the last synced source; the exact executed definition hash
is derived from the selected runtime's pinned recipe and emitted with each

get.description:
OAuth 2.0 Authorization Endpoint.

The end user must hold an authenticated Introspection session — resolved via
``scoped_auth`` (the ``intro_cp_session`` cookie on a browser redirect, or a
bearer token for the programmatic DP flow). Creates an authorization code and
redirects to the client's registered redirect URI.

Security:
- Validates client_id against registered clients
- Validates redirect_uri against client's allowed patterns
- Supports PKCE for enhanced security
- Binds state to authorization code

Typical flow:
1. Frontend has an authenticated OIDC session
2. Frontend calls this endpoint with the CP-issued bearer token
3. CP creates auth code, redirects to DP
4. DP exchanges code for access+refresh tokens

post.description:
RFC 8628 §3.1/§3.2 — device authorization request.

Unauthenticated by design: the user has not logged in yet (that is the
whole point of the CLI device flow). Only the first-party `cli` client
may start it. Returns a high-entropy opaque ``device_code`` (polled at
the token endpoint) and a short human ``user_code`` (typed into the
``/activate`` page).

Send a sign-in code to ``email`` for an Application's end user.

Unauthenticated, like the device flow: the user is not signed in yet. The
answer is the same ``202`` whether or not the email has an account, and the
route does no Zitadel I/O, so it cannot be used to enumerate users.

OAuth 2.0 Token Endpoint.

Supports:
- authorization_code: Exchange auth code for tokens (with PKCE verification)
- refresh_token: Get new access token using refresh token
- urn:ietf:params:oauth:grant-type:device_code: CLI device flow (RFC 8628)
- client_credentials: server-to-server Application auth (intro_app_/intro_sk_)

OAuth 2.0 Token Revocation (RFC 7009).

``session_id`` and ``org_id`` name the row. A session that backs a CP
cookie is revoked only with ``token``, its refresh token or the CP cookie
value, since its id is in its access token and a bare id would let anyone
who saw that token sign its person out. Every other session is revoked by
id, whatever ``token`` says, which is what every released SDK and data
plane sends. Session revocation is immediate - the next token refresh will
fail.

A first-party client or an Application client: a native Application's email-code session is refreshed with its
Application client_id (`_handle_refresh_token`), so its sign-out revokes with the same one.

get.description:
Return current user info from the session cookie.

Browser clients call this to check auth status and get user info
for the UI. Auth is resolved from the intro_cp_session cookie by
validate_auth — no token or session ID needed from the client.

Feature flags are evaluated server-side using trusted JWT context
(email, org_id, plan) so the browser cannot spoof targeting
attributes.

Logout: revoke CP session, clear cookie, redirect to IDP end_session.

Flow:
  1. Browser hits GET /v1/oidc/logout?redirect_uri=/sign-in (cookie sent automatically)
  2. CP reads cookie → looks up session → gets id_token, revokes session
  3. CP stores redirect_uri in a short-lived __oidc_logout cookie
  4. CP redirects to Zitadel end_session_endpoint with id_token_hint
     and post_logout_redirect_uri pointing to /v1/oidc/callback?logout
  5. Zitadel clears SSO session → redirects to /v1/oidc/callback?logout
  6. Callback reads __oidc_logout cookie → redirects browser to redirect_uri

A GET that a page on another site triggered would sign the member out of the
Control Plane and every plane, since a SameSite=Lax cookie still rides a
top-level navigation. The browser's ``Sec-Fetch-Site`` header names that
initiator, so a ``cross-site`` request is refused with the session intact.

ApplicationIdp.title: ApplicationIdp
ApplicationIdp.description:
A brokered upstream IdP for a federated Application (API response shape).

``id``, ``org_id``, ``created_at``, ``updated_at``, and ``deleted_at`` come
from ``OrgScopedEntity``. The client secret is transparently encrypted via
``EncryptedModelMixin``: in the database it lives only in the
``client_secret_encrypted`` BYTEA column (AES-256-GCM, AAD bound to the row's
identity), which API-facing selects omit entirely. The plaintext
``client_secret`` below is a write-only/decrypt-only carrier — it is ``None``
on every API read and is populated only by the repository's ``get_with_secret``
path (``from_encrypted``), consumed by the provisioning handler.

ApplicationIdpProvider.title: ApplicationIdpProvider
ApplicationIdpProvider.description:
Vendor label for the brokered customer IdP.

A UI hint that drives default issuer URLs / scopes per vendor; the federation
itself stays provider-agnostic and runs purely off issuer / client_id /
scopes. ``generic`` is any other OIDC issuer. This is the VENDOR, distinct
from Zitadel's protocol-level IdP type (which is OIDC for all of these).

``ZITADEL`` is the exception — not an external vendor but Introspection's
hosted built-in login for an spa application's end users: provisioning
enables Zitadel-native username/password registration on the per-federation
customers org instead of registering a custom upstream. No issuer, no
client credentials; the end user signs in (or registers) at the customers
org's hosted login and the brokered token-exchange path is unchanged.

``NEON`` (Neon Auth) is app-level only for now: the Postgres
``application_idp_provider`` enum type (created on main, not this branch)
does not yet include ``'neon'``, so persisting it requires a follow-up
``ALTER TYPE application_idp_provider ADD VALUE IF NOT EXISTS 'neon'``
migration on main. Until then, rows for Neon-backed federations carry the
``generic`` vendor label (the federation is provider-agnostic either way).

ApplicationIdpStatus.title: ApplicationIdpStatus
ApplicationIdpStatus.description:
Provisioning lifecycle of the brokered IdP in Zitadel.

A ``jwks`` application's direct federations have nothing to provision —
they are created ``ACTIVE`` immediately and never pass through
``PENDING`` / ``FAILED``.

ApplicationType.title: ApplicationType
ApplicationType.description:
The kind of OAuth client, chosen at creation and immutable.

The types are mutually exclusive, like OAuth client types elsewhere: each
offers one way in, so an end user never inherits a server credential's
scope ceiling and an app that needs two ways in registers two applications.
``service_account`` is the confidential server-to-server client; ``jwks``
exchanges the customer's own IdP JWT (RFC 8693) and runs no named grant;
``spa`` is Introspection's hosted login, optionally brokered; ``native`` is
email-code sign-in on Introspection accounts. Which identity providers each
type may attach is enforced in ``api/v1/application_idps.py``. See
applications-and-oauth.md §3.1 and native-email-auth.md.

Required for every provider except 'zitadel' (Introspection-hosted built-in login, which has no external issuer).

BrokeredIdpConfig.title: BrokeredIdpConfig
BrokeredIdpConfig.description:
Federated customer-IdP details for a `jwks` or `spa` app (applications-and-oauth.md
§5.0★ / §5.0★★). Provider-agnostic — any OIDC issuer (Okta, Supabase,
Auth0, …); the swap is which issuer/client you register here.

How the federation verifies its subject_token is a property of the
APPLICATION TYPE, not this payload: a `jwks` app's federation needs only
the issuer — the partner IdP's JWT is verified against its JWKS, nothing
is provisioned, and `client_id` / `client_secret` are not used. An `spa`
app's federation brokers through the per-app customers Zitadel org and
requires the partner IdP's `client_id` + `client_secret` (enforced in the
route, which knows the application).

The `client_secret` is write-only — it is encrypted at rest on the
`application_idps` row and forwarded to Zitadel once; it is never returned by
the API.

CallerContext.title: CallerContext
CallerContext.description:
Caller environment payload — segment.io-style observability data.

Carried alongside `identity` on `RunRequest` and persisted on the
session so it survives across all tasks the runner spawns. The Data
Plane stamps it onto each task as `metadata.caller`, which reaches the
sandbox in `INTROSPECTION_TASK_METADATA_JSON` along with the rest of
the task metadata. Echoed back on `RunnerSpec.runtime_context.caller`
for SDK display.

Distinct from `identity` — this payload is **not** consulted by
routing. `hash_key_fields` only walks `identity.user_id` /
`anonymous_id` / `conversation_id`. Mixing routing inputs into the
observability payload would be a privacy + stability footgun
(e.g. routing on IP).

Well-known fields are typed below; any additional fields the caller
passes (segment.io conventions: `app`, `device`, `os`, `campaign`,
`network`, `screen`, `timezone`, `traits`, or custom keys) ride
along verbatim via `extra="allow"`.

ClientRegistrationMethod.title: ClientRegistrationMethod
ClientRegistrationMethod.description:
How the platform identified itself to a custom OAuth provider.

Ordered by preference at discovery: a Client ID Metadata Document needs no
state on the provider and is the MCP default, dynamic registration is the
legacy path providers keep for older clients, and a pre-registered client
is what an operator supplies when the provider offers neither.

ConnectAuthorizeRequest.title: ConnectAuthorizeRequest
ConnectAuthorizeRequest.description:
What to mint a provider consent URL for (connect step 1).

A POST because the call is not a read: it writes a single-use `state` into
Redis with a TTL, so two calls yield two different URLs and neither response
may be cached. The OAuth spec's own `/authorize` is a GET, but that endpoint
redirects a browser — this one returns JSON to a backend caller, which is
the same shape as Stripe's account links or Plaid's link tokens, both POSTs.

expires_in.title: Expires In
expires_in.description: Seconds the URL stays valid. It carries a single-use state, so a caller handing it to someone else — an SDK integrator putting it in front of their own user — needs to know it cannot be cached or shared indefinitely.

expires_at.title: Expires At
expires_at.description: Absolute expiry, the same deadline as `expires_in`. Both are returned because they answer different questions: a caller rendering a countdown wants the interval, and one persisting the URL wants a timestamp it can compare against later without having recorded when the response arrived.

ConnectAuthorizeResponse.description: The provider consent URL the caller opens to grant access (connect step 1).

is required alongside it) and authorized by the connector being connected.
Non-secret: the URL and any extra headers are the same values an operator
would put on `POST /v1/endpoints`; the provider token stays on the
connection and is injected at the egress.

ConnectorUpdate.title: ConnectorUpdate
ConnectorUpdate.description:
Partial update — only provided fields change.

``environment`` is deliberately absent: it is a create-time fact. A staging
and a production provider app are separate apps holding separate
credentials, and the provider keeps delivering to one URL — changing it
would repoint live connections at the wrong one.

``agent_member_id`` IS settable. It is the actor a channel session carries,
not its subject: the turn is minted as the channel member, who owns the
resulting task and files. Changing the actor redirects future delegation
and reassigns nothing.

The two secrets are **write-only**: accepted here, never present on any
response shape. They are settable after create because the registration
order requires it — a provider app is registered against the delivery URL,
which contains the connector id, so the row exists before the app does and
therefore before its credentials do. The create-time upsert deliberately
preserves sealed columns (its AAD is bound to a freshly-generated id), so
this is the only path that can fill them in, and the only path that can
replace a leaked one.

traffic from the posterior, so operators set neither a per-arm weight nor a
control flag. The incumbent (current production version) is simply whichever
runtime currently serves production for the group — out-of-sample traffic is
routed to it via normal production resolution, independent of the experiment.

ExperimentRoutingStrategy.title: ExperimentRoutingStrategy
ExperimentRoutingStrategy.description:
How CP picks an arm per runner request.

BETA_SAMPLE is the only strategy — a multi-armed bandit. It is per-request
Thompson sampling seeded by the identity token (reproducible) on every lane;
arms are symmetric (no special baseline). Production exposure is bounded by
the experiment's `sample_rate` (an out-of-sample subject is served the
group's normal production runtime, unattributed), not by a candidate-traffic
cap. In-sample subjects are pinned to one arm for the experiment's lifetime.
(Retained as a single-value enum so the row + API response keep a typed
strategy; hrw / round_robin were removed.)

ExperimentStatus.title: ExperimentStatus
ExperimentStatus.description:
Experiment lifecycle.

draft → arms can still be edited; routing is not live.
running → routing live; scorer updating posteriors + weights. At most one
    running experiment per (runtime group + environment); starting another
    while one is running is a 409 — end it first.
ended → operator concluded the experiment after reviewing the result
    (terminal; production changes only when the winning PR is merged).
cancelled → operator aborted before a winner (terminal).

ExperimentUpdate.title: ExperimentUpdate
ExperimentUpdate.description:
PATCH /v1/experiments/{id} — mutable fields.

Status transitions go through dedicated endpoints (start / end /
cancel); runtime_group_id and arms are immutable once the experiment is
running so live routing decisions can never become inconsistent. While
running, only description stays editable; goal_json and sample_rate are
fixed so accumulated evidence keeps a single measured objective and the
sampled population never shifts mid-experiment.

RecipeValidation.title: RecipeValidation
RecipeValidation.description:
Persisted validation result, separate from derived Recipe projections.

`diagnostics` carry the checker's per-file verdict detail (valid/invalid);
`error_message` says why a `failed` attempt could not run, mirroring the

RecipeValidationUpdate.description:
The only client-requestable validation transition.

Validation results remain worker-owned. A client may reset the state to
pending to request a fresh attempt, but it cannot manufacture a terminal
valid, invalid, or failed result.

RepositoryProvider.title: RepositoryProvider
RepositoryProvider.description:
Who serves a repository's Git, which decides how a client reaches it.

`introspection` is served by the project's own data plane, so a runtime
clones it with its own session token and needs no third-party credential.
The UI displays it as "Private Git". `github` needs an installation token
from the integration the row names.

identity.description: Caller identity. A stable identity makes normal Runtime traffic eligible for experiment sampling and is required when targeting an Experiment directly. Normal Runtime traffic without one falls back to the active environment Runtime.

environment.description: Environment whose bindings apply. Human member sessions may override their credential environment; agent credentials remain environment-bound.

recipe_id.title: Recipe Id
recipe_id.description: Select one Runtime version for initial task creation. The Recipe must belong to the Runtime group identified by the URL Runtime id. This bypasses automatic experiment and active-environment routing when the runner is minted; subsequent task runs retain the group's sticky/latest policy.

bindings_required.title: Bindings Required
bindings_required.description: Require every application binding to materialize. Set false for operator testing where identity-dependent bindings may be reported as unavailable.

caller.description: Optional caller environment payload (segment.io-style) — IP, user_agent, locale, library, page, plus any extra fields. Persisted on the session and stamped onto every task the runner spawns as `metadata.caller`. Not consulted by routing.

agent_name.title: Agent Name
agent_name.description: Optional entrypoint agent to run. Omit to use the runtime's default agent.

scope.title: Scope
scope.description: Space-separated scopes to mint onto the runner JWT, capped to the runner-grantable set (tasks/files/shares read+write, conversations:read, events:read, metrics:read, telemetry:write). Omit for the legacy full-access runner. Use a narrow scope when the runner token is handed to a browser.

RunRequest.title: RunRequest
RunRequest.description:
Customer-facing body for `POST /v1/runtimes/{id}/run` and
`POST /v1/experiments/{id}/run`.

Scope fields (org_id, project_id, member_id, task_id) come from
auth and the URL — the customer only supplies their identity, an
optional caller, and an optional TTL override. The route
wraps this into a full `RuntimeContext` for the internal service
layer.

runtime_group_id.title: Runtime Group Id
runtime_group_id.description: Runtime group binding for latest/sticky resolution.

experiment_id.title: Experiment Id
experiment_id.description: Set when CP picked the arm via an experiment.

recipe_id.title: Recipe Id
recipe_id.description: Recipe pin on the resolved runtime.

arm_label.title: Arm Label
arm_label.description: Operator-facing arm label, populated when via /experiments/{id}/run.

agent_name.title: Agent Name
agent_name.description: Default entrypoint agent selected for this runner session.

identity.description: Identity the session is bound to (echo of the request input).

caller.description: Echo of the caller's caller if one was supplied on the /run request. None when the request didn't include one.

RunnerContextSummary.title: RunnerContextSummary
RunnerContextSummary.description:
Runtime context surfaced on `RunnerSpec.runtime_context`.

Mixes server-resolved fields (runtime_id, experiment_id, recipe,
arm_label) with caller-supplied echoes (identity, caller).
All runner-context-shaped fields live here so the SDK customer
reads `runner.runtime_context.*` for everything related to this
runner's session.

Snapshots the state at session-create time; not updated on refresh
(the underlying session's runtime context is immutable once
created).

endpoint.title: Endpoint
endpoint.description: Public URL of the DP, e.g. `https://api.gcp01.introspection.dev`.

RunnerDeployment.title: RunnerDeployment
RunnerDeployment.description:
Public deployment info surfaced on `RunnerSpec.deployment`.

Identifies the DP the runner is bound to. The SDK uses `endpoint`
as the base URL for `runner.tasks.*` / `runner.files.*` calls;
`slug` + `region` are surfaced for dashboard display and support
triage ("which region did this runner land in?"). Sensitive
deployment fields (config, JWT private key, cloud credentials)
stay internal.

tags.title: Tags
tags.description: Tags to stamp on the `customer` member this identity mints, if it is new (docs/design/shared-tags.md §6). Access-bearing, so it is attenuated to the asserting agent member's own tags and applied on CREATE only — an existing member's tags are never changed here.

metadata.title: Metadata
metadata.description: Metadata to set on the `customer` member this identity names. Grants nothing, so unlike `tags` it applies to an existing member too: the keys are merged in and overwrite keys of the same name, including ones an admin set. Absent or empty changes nothing. A merge that would leave the member with more than 64 keys is skipped whole. Not carried on the access-token claims.

RunnerIdentity.title: RunnerIdentity
RunnerIdentity.description:
Caller identity captured at session creation time.

Drives consistent-hash routing for experiments and rides on the
materialised access-token claims so DP can stamp it onto
`task.metadata.identity` and forward as `TASK_USER_ID` /
`TASK_ANONYMOUS_ID` / `TASK_CONVERSATION_ID` sandbox env. The
harness picks it up as OTel resource attributes automatically.

session_id.title: Session Id
session_id.description: UUID7, used as Redis key + AGENT_SESSION_ID

deployment.description: DP the session is bound to. The SDK uses `deployment.endpoint` as the base URL for `runner.tasks.*` / `runner.files.*` calls. The customer never types a DP URL themselves — multi-DP routing falls out for free.

session_token.title: Session Token
session_token.description: Signed session_locator JWT — the customer's long-lived credential. SDK sends it as `Authorization: Bearer <token>` on every `runner.tasks.*` / `runner.files.*` call. DP recognises `type=session_locator`, looks up the session in its Redis cache, and materialises a short-lived access token transparently via the existing session_materializer Restate path.

runtime_context.description: Resolved runtime + identity context. Populated by the runner /run routes; left as the default empty summary for gateway/channel session creators that don't carry a runtime context.

RunnerSpec.title: RunnerSpec
RunnerSpec.description:
Response from `POST /v1/runtimes/{id}/run` and `/v1/experiments/{id}/run`.

Customer-facing wire shape. The SDK holds exactly one credential:
`session_token`. DP transparently materialises the per-request
access tokens it needs via the existing session_materializer
Restate path — the SDK doesn't see or manage them.

Sandbox-internal fields (access_token, refresh_token, egress
credentials map, sandbox bootstrap, DP-enforced limits, managed LLM
proxy) live on `InternalRunnerSpec` and are only returned from
`POST /internal/agent-sessions` on the CP→DP path. Keeping them
off the customer wire means a leaked `RunnerSpec` JSON can't
expose materialised JWTs, upstream API keys, repo installation
IDs, or LLM-spend authorization.

RuntimeImageBuildMetadata.title: RuntimeImageBuildMetadata
RuntimeImageBuildMetadata.description:
Public details for the Runtime's currently projected image build.

The stored JSONB also carries the internal ``attempt_id`` ordering cursor,
read here for writes that must stay on the current attempt but never
serialized; the DP projection request models it explicitly below.

RuntimeImageStatus.title: RuntimeImageStatus
RuntimeImageStatus.description:
Image build lifecycle, projected from the DP bake pipeline.

``pending`` = no bake recorded yet; ``queued`` = a bake claim is waiting
for a bake-pool slot; ``building`` = the bake is executing; ``ready`` /
``failed`` = terminal build outcomes. A dispatch cancelled before reaching
the bake gate projects back to ``pending``; a queued/building claim that
expires projects ``failed`` with its timeout reason. In either case the DP
may re-claim the content key on the next launch. ``skipped`` = the data
plane does not bake, so no warmup verdict will ever arrive; nothing on the
control plane records whether a plane bakes, so the plane reports it.

RuntimeLlmMode.title: RuntimeLlmMode

RuntimeMcpRequirement.title: RuntimeMcpRequirement
RuntimeMcpRequirement.description:
One declared MCP server requirement resolved for one Runtime environment.

Covers every `recipe.mcp_servers` declaration, whether or not it is
backed by a `runtime.connectors` entry — a requirement with no matching
connector slug simply skips the connector/connection resolution steps
and reports on binding state alone.

Non-secret by construction: identifiers, statuses and a resource URL —
never tokens or stored headers.

Applies to the whole group, not a single version.
